text:
Hi,
I think it's mostly because school math has to fit a fixed curriculum. You have standards, tests, and a lot of material, and the history of math doesn't usually count toward any of those things. So it gets treated as optional enrichment, or skipped when time runs short. Also, many teachers were trained in a very technical way, so they may not feel comfortable mixing in historical context unless they have studied it. Exams decide what gets taught, and history is rarely marked. It is usually a nice bonus, not a required part. That explains the separation.
I agree it could be more interesting. The story of how math developed can make concepts feel less arbitrary. I would not push it into every lesson, but a few well-placed examples are worth the trouble. If you have time, try one historical example tied to the current topic, not as a separate chapter.
Thanks
